summary: In this episode, Fathers Andrew Stephen Damick and Stephen De Young discuss the Holy Mystery of Ordination, the fourth in their series on the sacraments. They begin by exploring the biblical foundations of priesthood, starting with Adam as a prototype, then moving to Aaron and his sons, whose ordination is described in detail in Leviticus 8. They examine the symbolism of the high priest's vestments, the budding of Aaron's rod, and the role of the high priest as a throne guardian. The conversation then shifts to St. Dionysius the Areopagite and his writings on the celestial and ecclesiastical hierarchies, contrasting Eastern and Western interpretations. They emphasize that ordination is not about imparting an ontological change or power, but about God working through particular individuals for the good of the community. They also address questions about the priesthood of all believers, the nature of ordination as a gift, and the practical implications for clergy and laity alike.

entities.title: Aaron
entities.summary: The first high priest of Israel, brother of Moses, whose ordination is described in Leviticus 8 and whose rod budded as a sign of God's choice.

entities.title: Moses
entities.summary: The leader of Israel who officiated at Aaron's ordination, acting as the efficient of the ritual even though he was not a priest himself.

entities.title: St. Dionysius the Areopagite
entities.summary: A saint and author of the Celestial Hierarchy and Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, whose writings are used to understand the relationship between angelic and ecclesiastical orders.

entities.title: Leviticus 8
entities.summary: The chapter describing the ordination of Aaron and his sons, including washing, vesting, anointing, and sacrifices.

entities.title: Numbers 17
entities.summary: The account of Aaron's rod budding as a sign of God's choice of the Levitical priesthood.

entities.title: Numbers 18
entities.summary: The chapter where God explains Aaron's duties, including bearing the sins of the people and guarding the sanctuary.

concepts.title: Ordination as Gift
concepts.summary: Ordination is not a reward for personal merit or achievement, but a gift from God, given to specific individuals for the service of the community.

concepts.title: Priesthood of All Believers
concepts.summary: The collective priesthood of Israel and the Church is a communal calling to represent God to the world and the world to God, distinct from the ordained priesthood.

concepts.title: Throne Guardian
concepts.summary: The high priest, like the cherubim and seraphim, serves as a guardian of sacred space, protecting people from the danger of approaching God unworthily.

concepts.title: Bearing Sins
concepts.summary: The high priest bears the sins of the people, leading them in repentance and representing them before God, a role fulfilled perfectly by Christ.

concepts.title: Eastern vs. Western Reading of Dionysius
concepts.summary: The West has often read St. Dionysius through a Neoplatonic lens, seeing hierarchies as ontological, while the East reads them as functional, with grace understood as divine energies.

concepts.title: Ordination as Set Apart
concepts.summary: Ordination sets a person apart for a particular task, not changing their essence but dedicating them to a specific role within the community.

claims.text: Adam, placed in Eden, serves as a prototype of the priesthood, and his placement in the sanctuary is a kind of ordination.
Aaron, as high priest, is presented as a new Adam, and the tabernacle/temple imagery evokes paradise, with the high priest enabling reentry into God's presence.
The cross, like Aaron's rod, is a dead piece of wood that blossoms with new life, marking Christ as the great high priest and new Adam.
Ordination does not change a person's being; it sets them apart for a particular role, and the grace of God works through them functionally, not ontologically.
The primary job of the priest is to guard the sanctuary and protect the people from approaching God unworthily, which includes fencing the table at the Eucharist.
Repentance is not only individual but also collective; communities can sin and must repent corporately, and priests lead in this repentance.

scriptural_links.summary: Israel is called a kingdom of priests and a holy nation, which is discussed in relation to the collective priesthood.
The detailed account of Aaron's ordination, including washing, vesting, anointing, and sacrifices.
The budding of Aaron's rod as a sign of God's choice of the priesthood.
God explains Aaron's duties, including bearing sins and guarding the sanctuary.
The suffering servant passage is interpreted in light of the high priestly role of bearing sins, not as penal substitution.
Jesus' healing is seen as fulfillment of Isaiah 53, understood as bearing sins in the high priestly sense.
Paul's warning about approaching the Eucharist unworthily is used to support the priest's role as guardian of the table.

glossary.definition: A priestly garment, part of the high priest's vestments, with twelve stones representing the tribes of Israel.
Objects kept in the breastplate of the high priest, used for discerning God's will, though their exact nature is unknown.
A crown worn by the high priest with the name of Yahweh inscribed on a gold plate, symbolizing his role as representative of God.
A ritual in which an offering is waved before the Lord, often the priest's portion, symbolizing that it belongs to God and is given back.
A Greek term meaning 'deposit' or 'charge', used in the ordination service when the bishop gives the newly ordained priest the consecrated bread to guard.
